concepts.s: Postpartum hemorrhage is cumulative blood loss of 1000 mL or hypovolemia within 24 hours of birth, and it is treated with uterine massage, oxytocin, tranexamic acid within 3 hours, second-line uterotonics, and blood.

x.b:
• Definition: ACOG (Practice Bulletin 183): cumulative blood loss of 1000 mL or more, or blood loss with signs of hypovolemia, within 24 hours of birth. WHO uses more than 500 mL.
  • The 4 Ts: tone (atony, most common), tissue (retained placenta), trauma (lacerations, uterine rupture, inversion), thrombin (coagulopathy, DIC, amniotic fluid embolism).
  • Young healthy patients compensate; hypotension is a late sign. Secondary PPH occurs from 24 hours to 12 weeks (retained products, endometritis).

• Quantify blood loss; vital signs and shock index.
  • CBC, fibrinogen (low fibrinogen predicts severe PPH), coagulation, type and crossmatch, viscoelastic testing if available.
  • Inspect the placenta and the genital tract; bedside ultrasound for retained tissue or intraperitoneal blood.

Doses from the EB Medicine PPH rapid reference (citing ACOG PB 183 and WHO).

  1. Call for help, obstetrics, anesthesia, massive transfusion protocol; bimanual uterine massage; empty the bladder.
  2. Oxytocin (first line): 10 to 40 units in 500 to 1000 mL IV infusion, or 10 units IM. Avoid rapid IV push (hypotension).
  3. Tranexamic acid: 1 g IV over 10 minutes, with a second 1 g dose if bleeding continues after 30 minutes; most benefit within 3 hours of birth.
  4. Methylergonovine: 0.2 mg IM every 2 to 4 hours; contraindicated in hypertension and preeclampsia; never IV.
  5. Carboprost: 250 mcg IM every 15 minutes, up to 8 doses; contraindicated in asthma.
  6. Misoprostol: 800 to 1000 mcg rectally, 600 mcg PO, or 800 mcg sublingually.
  7. Blood products in balanced ratios; replace fibrinogen.
  8. Mechanical and surgical: intrauterine balloon tamponade, repair lacerations, manual removal of retained placenta, uterine artery embolization, compression sutures, hysterectomy.

Trap: Waiting for hypotension to recognize hemorrhage. By the time blood pressure falls, the patient may have lost a large share of blood volume; use quantified blood loss and the shock index.
  • Giving methylergonovine to a hypertensive or preeclamptic patient, or carboprost to an asthmatic.
  • Missing uterine inversion (shock out of proportion, mass at the introitus) or a concealed hematoma.
  • ED deliveries with PPH need obstetric and anesthesia involvement and usually ICU or labor and delivery admission.

cards.q: How does ACOG define postpartum hemorrhage?
cards.a: Cumulative blood loss of 1000 mL or more, or blood loss with hypovolemia, within 24 hours of birth.

cards.q: What is the tranexamic acid dose and timing in PPH?
cards.a: 1 g IV over 10 minutes within 3 hours of birth, repeating 1 g after 30 minutes if bleeding continues.

cards.q: What is the carboprost dose and its key contraindication?
cards.a: 250 mcg IM every 15 minutes up to 8 doses; contraindicated in asthma.

cards.q: What is the methylergonovine dose and key contraindication?
cards.a: 0.2 mg IM every 2 to 4 hours; contraindicated in hypertension and preeclampsia.

cards.q: What are the 4 Ts of PPH?
cards.a: Tone, tissue, trauma, and thrombin.

concepts.s: Stratify well-appearing febrile infants by age band and inflammatory markers: full workup and admission for 8 to 21 days, markers-driven LP decisions for 22 to 28 days, and selective LP for 29 to 60 days.

x.b:
• Scope of the 2021 AAP guideline (Pantell and colleagues, Pediatrics): well-appearing infants 8 to 60 days old, born at 37 to 42 weeks, with a temperature of 38.0 C or higher.
  • Exclusions: preterm, ill appearance, focal bacterial infection, clinical bronchiolitis, high HSV suspicion, immunocompromise, complicated neonatal course, technology dependence, recent vaccination within 48 hours.
  • HSV red flags: maternal genital lesions or fever around delivery, vesicles, seizures, hypothermia, mucosal ulcers, CSF pleocytosis without organisms, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, elevated ALT.
  • Ill-appearing infants of any age get full workup, broad antibiotics, and admission.

• Inflammatory markers (IMs) considered abnormal (First10EM summary of AAP 2021): procalcitonin above 0.5 ng/mL, CRP 20 mg/L or higher (AAP REVISE II matrix), ANC above 4000 to 5200 per mm3, and temperature above 38.5 C. Procalcitonin plus ANC or CRP is preferred; do not use WBC.
  • Urinalysis in all; catheter culture if the UA is positive.
  • Blood culture in all.
  • LP: required at 8 to 21 days; should be done at 22 to 28 days if any IM is abnormal and may be done if normal; may be done at 29 to 60 days if IMs are abnormal.

Age bands per AAP 2021 (UMEM and First10EM summaries); drug choices and doses from the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia febrile infant pathway.

  1. 8 to 21 days: UA, blood culture, CSF; start empiric antibiotics regardless of results; admit. CHOP lists ampicillin plus ceftazidime (ceftazidime 50 mg/kg every 8 hours after day 7; ampicillin 75 mg/kg every 6 hours for 8 to 28 days at meningitic dosing), plus acyclovir 20 mg/kg every 8 hours when HSV is possible.
  2. 22 to 28 days: UA, blood culture, IMs. Abnormal IMs: LP and antibiotics, admit. Normal UA, normal IMs, and normal CSF: may go home after a parenteral antibiotic dose with reassessment within 24 hours, using shared decision-making. No CSF obtained: admit, with the option to observe off antibiotics (AAP REVISE II matrix). CHOP avoids ceftriaxone at 28 days and younger, while the AAP REVISE II matrix shows a single ceftriaxone dose for discharge at 22 to 28 days; follow local pathway.
  3. 29 to 60 days: UA, blood culture, IMs. Normal IMs and negative UA: home without antibiotics, follow-up within 24 hours (AAP REVISE II matrix). Normal IMs and positive UA: oral antibiotics (CHOP: cephalexin 50 mg/kg/day divided every 8 hours) and follow-up. Abnormal IMs: consider LP; if CSF is unobtainable or uninterpretable, parenteral antibiotics with observation in hospital or at home per AAP (CHOP: ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg every 24 hours if well with no pleocytosis, every 12 hours if pleocytosis or ill appearance, plus vancomycin for meningitis).

Trap: Applying the guideline to an ill-appearing, preterm, or bronchiolitic infant. It covers only well-appearing term infants, and everyone else needs full evaluation.
  • Giving antibiotics without CSF in an infant 22 to 28 days or one with abnormal markers creates a partially treated meningitis that cannot be excluded.
  • Missing HSV in the first 3 weeks; it can present without vesicles.
  • A positive respiratory viral test does not remove the risk of UTI.
  • Every discharge requires reliable follow-up within about 24 hours and clear return precautions.

cards.q: Which infants does the 2021 AAP febrile infant guideline cover?
cards.a: Well-appearing term infants 8 to 60 days old with temperature 38.0 C or higher.

cards.q: What procalcitonin and CRP values count as abnormal inflammatory markers?
cards.a: Procalcitonin above 0.5 ng/mL and CRP 20 mg/L or higher.

cards.q: What is the AAP 2021 approach for a well-appearing febrile infant 8 to 21 days old?
cards.a: UA, blood culture, and CSF; empiric antibiotics; admit.

cards.q: Which infants 29 to 60 days may go home without antibiotics?
cards.a: Those with normal inflammatory markers and a negative UA, with follow-up within 24 hours.

cards.q: Why is ceftriaxone avoided in infants 28 days and younger?
cards.a: It is not recommended in that age group (it displaces bilirubin and interacts with calcium), so pathways use ampicillin with ceftazidime or cefepime.

concepts.s: Pediatric arrest is usually respiratory, so prioritize oxygenation and ventilation, give weight-based epinephrine and shocks per PALS 2025, give 10 to 20 mL/kg fluid boluses with reassessment in shock, and rehydrate most gastroenteritis orally with ondansetron.

x.b:
• Pediatric assessment triangle: appearance, work of breathing, circulation to skin.
  • Compensated shock: tachycardia, prolonged capillary refill, cool extremities with a normal BP; hypotension is a late, pre-arrest sign.
  • Bradycardia in a child is usually hypoxic; PALS 2025 starts CPR for heart rate below 60 with poor perfusion despite oxygenation and ventilation.
  • Dehydration (OHSU pathway, clinical dehydration scale scoring appearance, eyes, mucous membranes, tears 0 to 2 each): 0 none, 1 to 4 mild, 5 to 8 moderate to severe.

• Weight: measured, or a length-based tape; every dose depends on it.
  • Point-of-care glucose in every sick child and in moderate or severe dehydration, altered mentation, or lethargy.
  • Electrolytes for moderate to severe dehydration, IV rehydration, or abnormal history (very young age, prolonged illness).
  • Look for the H's and T's in arrest: hypovolemia, hypoxia, acidosis, hypoglycemia, hypo- or hyperkalemia, hypothermia, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, thrombosis.

Cardiac arrest (2025 AHA PALS cardiac arrest algorithm):

  • CPR at 100 to 120 per minute, depth at least one third of the chest, 15:2 with two rescuers before puberty, 30:2 with one rescuer or after puberty; with an advanced airway, one breath every 2 to 3 seconds.
  • Epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg IV or IO (0.1 mL/kg of 0.1 mg/mL), maximum 1 mg, every 3 to 5 minutes.
  • Defibrillation for VF or pulseless VT: 2 J/kg, then 4 J/kg, then 4 J/kg or more up to 10 J/kg or the adult dose.
  • Amiodarone 5 mg/kg IV or IO (maximum 300 mg first dose, 150 mg later doses), up to 3 doses, or lidocaine 1 mg/kg.

Bradycardia (2025 AHA PALS bradycardia algorithm): epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg (maximum 1 mg); atropine 0.02 mg/kg (minimum 0.1 mg, maximum single dose 0.5 mg) for increased vagal tone or primary AV block, may repeat once; consider pacing.

SVT (2025 Red Cross PALS card): adenosine 0.1 mg/kg rapid push (maximum 6 mg), then 0.2 mg/kg (maximum 12 mg); synchronized cardioversion 0.5 to 1 J/kg, then 2 J/kg.

Septic shock (2025 Red Cross PALS septic shock card): 10 to 20 mL/kg balanced crystalloid boluses with reassessment after each, repeated to a maximum of 60 mL/kg, or up to 40 mL/kg over the first hour where intensive care access is limited; 5 to 10 mL/kg in cardiac dysfunction; stop for signs of fluid overload. Epinephrine 0.1 to 1 mcg/kg/min or norepinephrine 0.05 to 2 mcg/kg/min; antibiotics within 60 minutes.

Dehydration (OHSU pathway):

  1. Ondansetron for children 6 months and older: oral 1 to 2 mg (7 to 14 kg), 2 to 4 mg (15 to 26 kg), 8 mg (27 kg or more); IV 0.1 to 0.2 mg/kg, maximum 8 mg.
  2. Oral rehydration in small frequent aliquots: under 10 kg, 5 mL every 5 minutes for 20 minutes then 10 mL every 5 minutes; 10 kg or more, 10 mL then 20 mL every 5 minutes; 30 kg or more, 30 mL every 5 minutes for 40 minutes then 60 mL; reassess at 30 to 60 minutes.
  3. IV rehydration for severe dehydration or failed oral trial: 20 mL/kg normal saline, up to two boluses with reassessment; 10 mL/kg for neonates, cardiac, frail, or malnourished infants.
  4. Hypoglycemia (glucose below 70 mg/dL in children over 6 months): D10W 4 to 5 mL/kg (2 to 5 mL/kg elsewhere in the same pathway), recheck in 30 minutes, then glucose-containing maintenance fluid.

Trap: Dosing by guess. Mental arithmetic under pressure causes tenfold errors; use a length-based system or weight-based reference and read doses aloud.
  • Atropine is not first-line for hypoxic bradycardia; ventilate and oxygenate, then epinephrine.
  • Unchecked fluid boluses in septic children without ICU support can harm (FEAST trial); reassess after each.
  • Skipping the glucose check in a lethargic dehydrated toddler.
  • Dehydration discharge: tolerates oral fluids, caregivers can continue ORS, vital signs normal, mental status at baseline.

cards.q: What is the PALS 2025 epinephrine dose in pediatric cardiac arrest?
cards.a: 0.01 mg/kg IV or IO (0.1 mL/kg of 0.1 mg/mL), maximum 1 mg, every 3 to 5 minutes.

cards.q: What defibrillation energies does PALS 2025 use for pediatric VF?
cards.a: 2 J/kg, then 4 J/kg, then 4 J/kg or more up to 10 J/kg or the adult dose.

cards.q: What is the pediatric amiodarone dose in shock-refractory VF?
cards.a: 5 mg/kg IV or IO, up to 3 doses (maximum 300 mg first dose).

cards.q: What are the pediatric adenosine doses for SVT?
cards.a: 0.1 mg/kg (maximum 6 mg), then 0.2 mg/kg (maximum 12 mg).

cards.q: What pediatric atropine dose limits apply?
cards.a: 0.02 mg/kg, minimum 0.1 mg, maximum single dose 0.5 mg.
